extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of media/journalism
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic explanation of the term 'media circus' describing how to recognize and contextualize excessive or sensational media coverage, with historical notes and many illustrative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive or out-of-proportion media coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Media circus is a colloquial metaphor or idiom describing a news event for which the level of media coverage—measured by such factors as the number of reporters at the scene and the amount of material broadcast or published—is perceived to be excessive or out of proportion to the event being covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as the primary definitional test: ask whether coverage volume (reporters, broadcasts, published material) is disproportionate to the intrinsic newsworthiness of the event. The term functions as a critique of coverage rather than the event itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement factors: number of reporters and amount of material
rubrics_metrics.description: Level of media coverage is measured by such factors as the number of reporters at the scene and the amount of material broadcast or published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete indicators include presence of news media satellite up-link trucks, many photojournalists, frequent airtime or large amounts of published content. High counts on these measures increase likelihood the situation will be labeled a media circus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensationalistic coverage as an amplifying factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage that is sensationalistic can add to the perception the event is the subject of a media circus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess tone and style: sensationalistic framing, emotionalized language, emphasis on spectacle or gore, and infotainment techniques amplify perceptions of a media circus even if raw coverage volume is moderate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media feeding frenzy / recursive media coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: It can also be called a media feeding frenzy or just media frenzy, especially when the media coverage itself is covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for recursive dynamics where outlets report on other outlets' coverage, competitive chasing for scoops, and breathless repetition — these feedback loops are characteristic of a feeding frenzy variant of media circus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison to spectacle and pageantry (critique function)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term is meant to critique the coverage of the event by comparing it to the spectacle and pageantry of a circus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret usage as evaluative: calling something a 'media circus' signals critique of prioritizing spectacle over substance. Historical and cultural examples (e.g., films like Ace in the Hole) illustrate how media practices can create or exacerbate spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common triggers and typical contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain types of events are repeatedly described as media circuses, including high-profile trials, disappearances, celebrity life/death/funerals, sensational crimes, rescue operations, political scandals, and large-scale disasters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether coverage amounts to a media circus, consider event type and historical precedent: e.g., famous trials (O. J. Simpson, Casey Anthony), celebrity funerals (Jade Goody), rescues (Chilean miners, baby Jessica), disappearances (Madeleine McCann), or scandals (Lewinsky, phone hacking). A pattern of intense, sustained, and spectacle-driven coverage across these contexts supports the label.
